title: Summary functions and missing values (NA) in R
breadcrumb: Module 9 · R Programming · Summary functions and NA handling
objectives: Use common summary functions such as sum, mean, median, min, max and range.
Recognise how NA affects summaries and how na.rm=TRUE changes results.
Distinguish length, sum(!is.na(x)) and complete-case counts.
Interpret logical summaries and missing-value tests.
Avoid common NA, NaN and Inf output traps.

prereq.name: Descriptive statistics
prereq.why: Summary functions calculate common descriptive measures.

prereq.name: Logical vectors
prereq.why: is.na() produces logical indicators for missing entries.

traps: Most arithmetic summaries return NA when an input contains NA unless na.rm=TRUE is used.
na.rm=TRUE removes missing values for that calculation; it does not modify the original vector.
is.na(x) returns a logical vector; sum(is.na(x)) counts missing entries.
NaN is also treated as missing by is.na().
mean(x) and median(x) are different summaries.
range(x) returns two endpoints; diff(range(x)) gives the spread.

sheet: sum(x), mean(x), median(x), min(x), max(x) summarise numeric vectors.
range(x) returns c(min,max); diff(range(x)) gives max−min.
NA denotes a missing value; arithmetic involving NA generally propagates NA.
Use na.rm=TRUE to omit missing values for a summary.
na.rm=TRUE does not change the original vector.
is.na(x) identifies NA and NaN entries.
length(x) counts all positions, including NA.
na.rm=TRUE does not remove Inf or -Inf.
cards: Omit missing values for this calculation
tricks: Check for NA before computing a summary.
Do not assume na.rm removes Inf.
shortcuts: Compute the requested summary on that reduced set.
Keep length and observed count distinct.
Check whether the question asks count or value.
remember: na.rm=TRUE omits NA for one calculation.

howto: Inspect the vector for missing entries. Identify whether the question asks for a summary, missing count or observed count. Apply na.rm=TRUE only when required, and remember it does not mutate the original vector or remove infinite values.

scenes.title: What is a summary function?
body: Summary functions reduce a vector to one or a few descriptive values.
mean() calculates the arithmetic average; median() is the middle ordered value; min() and max() give endpoints.
range() returns both endpoints, not their difference. The statistical range is diff(range(x)).

refresh: NA is R's marker for a missing value. Many arithmetic summaries propagate NA by default because the missing observation prevents the complete calculation from being determined.
Do not silently replace NA with zero. Decide whether the question asks for a missingness count, a complete-case summary, or a different missing-data treatment, and state the rule being used.

items.recall: Omit missing values for that calculation.
refresh: The argument na.rm=TRUE tells a summary function to omit missing values while performing that particular calculation. It does not rewrite the vector or permanently delete any observations.
If the original vector contains five positions including two NA entries, length remains five after a mean call with na.rm=TRUE. A later function call still sees the original missing entries.

items.ask: How do you count observed entries?
refresh: is.na(x) creates a logical indicator for missing values. Negating that indicator identifies observed entries, and sum counts the TRUE values as one each.
Keep the three counts distinct: length(x) counts all positions, sum(is.na(x)) counts missing positions, and sum(!is.na(x)) counts observed positions. These quantities add to the vector length.

ask.q: Which function gives the middle ordered value?
ask.nudge: It is robust to extreme values.

scenes.title: Missing values affect calculations
body: NA represents a missing value. A calculation that depends on an unknown observation commonly returns NA.
For x=c(2,NA,6), mean(x) is NA, while mean(x,na.rm=TRUE) is 4.
na.rm=TRUE omits missing values for that call only; it does not edit x.

scenario.title: A researcher summarises a partial response vector
body: A researcher has responses 2, NA and 6. The mean is unavailable under the default missing-value rule, but can be computed from observed responses with na.rm=TRUE.
The number of observed responses is two, while length(x) remains three.

The analyst should report the number of observed responses alongside the summary so readers can see how many values contributed to it. Missingness counts should be calculated separately from the statistic itself. The original vector should remain intact, because a later analysis may need to inspect which observations were missing or apply a different treatment.
scenario.q: What is the mean of observed values?

ask.q: Does na.rm=TRUE permanently remove NA from x?
ask.nudge: It is an argument to the summary call.

blocks.body: mean(x,na.rm=TRUE), sum(x,na.rm=TRUE), min(x,na.rm=TRUE) omit NA values for that calculation.
is.na(x) returns TRUE for NA and NaN entries.
sum(is.na(x)) counts missing entries; sum(!is.na(x)) counts observed entries.

ask.q: How do you count NA values?
ask.nudge: Apply is.na() and sum the TRUE values.

scenes.title: Compute summaries with missing values
scenes.problem: For x=c(2,NA,6,NA,10), find length(x), sum(is.na(x)), sum(!is.na(x)) and mean(x,na.rm=TRUE).

steps.why: NA still occupies a vector position.
na.rm=TRUE omits NA for this calculation.

items.a: Logical vector identifying NA and NaN.
Number of positions, including missing values.

scenes.title: NA, NaN and Inf are not interchangeable

blocks.body: is.na() is TRUE for both NA and NaN.
Inf and -Inf are infinite values, not missing values; na.rm=TRUE does not remove them.
Use is.na() for missingness. Use is.finite() when finite values are required.

scenes.title: Count observed values
scenes.objective: Separate vector length from complete observations.
scenes.problem: For x=c(NA,4,NA,8,10), find length(x) and the number of observed values.
hints: Count the FALSE entries in is.na(x).
scenes.check: There are five positions, two missing and three observed.

solution.why: These are the three entries that are not NA.
The question asks for the number of non-missing entries, not their mean.
The original vector still has five positions.

blocks.body: The mean uses every observed value and is sensitive to extreme observations.
The median is the middle ordered value (or average of two middle values for an even count). It is less sensitive to extremes.
For 1, 3, 100, the mean is 104/3, while the median is 3.

ask.q: Which summary is less affected by one extreme observation?
ask.nudge: It is based on the middle order statistic.

scenes.title: A summary drill with NA
scenes.problem: For x=c(1,NA,3,9), find sum(x,na.rm=TRUE), mean(x,na.rm=TRUE) and median(x,na.rm=TRUE).
hints: Divide by 3 for the mean; the middle ordered value is the median.
scenes.check: All summaries use the three observed values.

scenario.title: A field survey with missing entries
body: A field survey records 5, 7, NA, 9 and NA. The analyst needs the mean of observed values and the number of missing responses.
The observed mean uses na.rm=TRUE; the missing count uses sum(is.na(x)).

The analyst should report the number of observed responses alongside the summary so readers can see how many values contributed to it. Missingness counts should be calculated separately from the statistic itself. The original vector should remain intact, because a later analysis may need to inspect which observations were missing or apply a different treatment.
scenario.q: How many observations are available for the mean?

solution.why: na.rm=TRUE omits the one missing entry for these summaries.
Divide the sum by three; the middle ordered value is 3.

items.why: NaN is treated as missing by is.na().

ask.q: What is the difference between length(x) and sum(!is.na(x))?
ask.nudge: One counts positions; the other counts observed values.

scenes.title: The summary-function checklist
body: Use mean, median, min, max, sum and range for descriptive summaries.
NA propagates through many summaries unless na.rm=TRUE is used.
na.rm=TRUE omits missing values for that call only; it does not mutate x or remove Inf.
is.na(x) detects NA and NaN; sum(is.na(x)) counts missing entries.
length(x) includes NA; sum(!is.na(x)) counts observed values.
range returns endpoints; diff(range(x)) gives the statistical range.

ask.q: Give two expressions to count missing and observed values.
ask.nudge: Use sum with is.na and its negation.
